issues.legal_issue: A person who lawfully cultivates agricultural land under authority derived from a mortgagee may qualify as a deemed tenant even without authority derived directly from the owner.
material_facts: The land belonged to the owners and was in the possession of a mortgagee.
The mortgagee inducted the cultivator as a tenant, and the cultivator was lawfully cultivating the land on the relevant date.
The cultivator did not fall within any of the categories excluded from deemed tenancy.
The owners obtained possession through execution of an award without an order under the statutory tenancy procedure.
issues.conclusion: The cultivator qualified as a deemed tenant and was entitled to the protection of the tenancy statute, notwithstanding that his authority to cultivate derived from the mortgagee rather than directly from the owners.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(18) and 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a person lawfully cultivating land belonging to another is deemed a tenant if the land is not cultivated personally by its owner and the person is not within the exceptions in section 4(a), (b), or (c). The statute does not require the cultivator's authority to derive directly from the owner. Its protective purpose would be unduly restricted by importing that requirement. Although under the ordinary rule of the Transfer of Property Act a tenant inducted by a mortgagee in possession ordinarily loses that right when the mortgage ends, that rule does not govern the statutory status conferred on a person lawfully cultivating agricultural land.

predicates.agricultural_tenancy_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person cultivating agricultural land qualifies for statutory tenant status.
predicates.lawfully_cultivates_another_persons_land: The person cultivates land belonging to someone else lawfully.
predicates.cultivation_authority_is_derivative: The person's authority to cultivate comes through someone other than the landowner.
predicates.within_excluded_categories: The person belongs to a category excluded from deemed tenancy.

issues.definition: When a statutory tenant-status dispute concerns someone who lawfully cultivates another person's land under derivative authority and is not within an excluded category, that person qualifies as a deemed tenant.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant inducted by a mortgagee in possession is not excluded from deemed-tenant status merely because the statutory exceptions exclude a mortgagee in possession.
material_facts: A mortgagee in possession inducted a tenant to cultivate the land in the ordinary course of management.
The cultivator was a tenant of the mortgagee, not the mortgagee in possession or a transferee of the mortgagee's total rights.
The cultivator was lawfully cultivating the land and did not fall within the other specified exceptions.
issues.conclusion: The exception for a mortgagee in possession did not apply to the tenant inducted by the mortgagee, who could be deemed a tenant of the landowner after redemption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(c) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, excludes a mortgagee in possession from deemed-tenant status because granting that status to the mortgagee would conflict with the mortgagee's fiduciary character. The exclusion does not extend to a tenant inducted by the mortgagee in possession in the ordinary course of management. The statute's purpose supports treating that tenant as a deemed tenant upon redemption.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court may exercise supervisory jurisdiction when revenue authorities refuse to address the unlawful dispossession of a tenant whose possession was obtained without the required statutory order.
material_facts: The landlord obtained possession of land held by a tenant through execution of an award, without an order from the designated revenue officer.
The tenant sought restoration of possession under the tenancy statute.
The revenue authorities rejected the tenant's application and the ensuing challenges.
The tenant sought supervisory review of the revenue tribunal's decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was competent to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 227 because the tenant had been unlawfully dispossessed and the revenue authorities had illegally refused to exercise their jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, prohibits a landlord from obtaining possession of land held by a tenant except under an order of the designated revenue officer. Where possession is obtained without that order and the revenue authorities refuse to exercise jurisdiction to assist the dispossessed tenant, the question is jurisdictional and the High Court may intervene under Article 227 of the Constitution.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_revenue_decision: The proceeding asks the High Court to supervise a decision of a revenue authority.
predicates.tenant_unlawfully_dispossessed: A tenant was deprived of possession unlawfully.
predicates.possession_obtained_without_required_rev: The landlord obtained possession without the order required from the designated revenue authority.
predicates.revenue_authorities_refused_to_exercise_: The revenue authorities refused to exercise their jurisdiction to provide relief to the dispossessed tenant.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a revenue decision following a tenant's unlawful dispossession without the required revenue order and the revenue authorities' refusal to exercise jurisdiction, the High Court may intervene supervisorially.
